chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ali ibn Atiyya, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I was in his presence and a man asked him about a man from whom something comes out due to his anger, will Allah hold him responsible for it? So he said: Allah is more benevolent than to tie down His servant. And in a copy from Abu Al-Hasan Al-Awwal (peace be upon him): to coerce His servant.

key_terms.يَسْتَغْلِقَ: tie down / bind tightly (metaphor for strict accountability)

ai.seo_question: Does Allah punish a person for involuntary bodily functions caused by anger?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of *al-ghalib* (dominant state) versus *al-khasis* (specific state), clarifying that involuntary bodily emissions during anger are excused from ritual impurity or punishment. The variation in the text between *yastaghligh* (to close up/seal) and *yastaligh* (to diminish/reduce) reflects scholarly debate on whether divine mercy completely negates accountability or merely lessens it, underscoring the attribute of *Al-Karim* (The Generous).
